title: 1990s welfare reform reduced the decline in voting among exposed low-income women
source_unit: Low-income U.S. women observed in Current Population Survey Voting and Registration Supplements during 1990s welfare reform

observations.period: 1990–2004 CPS Voting and Registration Supplements; NBER Working Paper issued 2016

denominator.unit: repeated CPS state-year study frame; abstract does not state one pooled respondent denominator

voting_effect.value: about 4 percentage points higher voting relative to less-exposed comparison women, approximately 10% relative to baseline
voting_effect.unit: percentage points and relative-to-baseline change in voting participation

registration_and_voting_scope.value: effects largely confined to presidential elections

state_and_policy_heterogeneity.value: stronger in Democratic states and states with stronger work-incentive policies
state_and_policy_heterogeneity.unit: reported heterogeneity by political and policy context

proposed_pathway.value: appeared to operate through employment, education, and income
proposed_pathway.unit: reported mediation pattern; not a same-person mechanism ledger

observations.method: NBER Working Paper 22052 uses November Current Population Survey Voting and Registration Supplements from 1990–2004 and changes in welfare policy across states and over time, with comparison groups of women less exposed to welfare reform, to estimate voting registration and participation effects.
observations.uncertainty: This is a policy-exposure difference-in-differences design, not random assignment or a direct measure of individual benefit receipt. The abstract does not retain the full sample, policy exposure construction, parallel-trend diagnostics, or exact mediator estimates. Voting is not trust, approval, attribution, or broader civic action.
observations.subgroup: Low-income women at risk of relying on welfare, with heterogeneity by state political context and strength of work incentives.
observations.counterinterpretation: The positive voting result may reflect employment, education, income, composition, state policy environments, or selection into exposure together; it cannot be directly compared as an opposite estimate to the EITC employment-instrument paper without harmonizing treatment, population, period, and estimand.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI and working-paper metadata identify the study and authors.
Published Economic Inquiry version identifies the peer-reviewed article and reports the corresponding welfare-reform voting estimates.

boundary: This is a U.S. welfare-reform policy-exposure estimate for low-income women's voting, not a universal work effect, a contemporaneous cash-transfer effect, or a complete political-trust and institutional-legitimacy pathway.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official NBER Working Paper 22052 page downloaded and hashed; title, date, CPS Voting and Registration Supplement design, 1990–2004 frame, voting magnitude, presidential-election scope, state heterogeneity, and proposed mediators checked against the abstract.
